name: runas /netonly - Inject AD Creds on Windows
description: Spawns a new process (typically PowerShell) with AD credentials injected for network authentication, without requiring the machine to be domain-joined or the current user to be that account interactively. Used to run domain tools (PowerView, Mimikatz DCSync, etc.) AS a domain user from a workgroup machine or from a different user context.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY /NETONLY ===
runas /netonly creates a LOGON32_LOGON_NEW_CREDENTIALS logon session:
  - The spawned process runs AS you locally (same local token)
  - But when the process makes NETWORK connections, it uses the injected credentials
  - Domain-joined check is bypassed — works from any Windows machine

This means you can run Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync or PowerView from a non-domain-joined
Windows host and it will authenticate to the DC using the creds you injected.

=== KEY USE CASES ===
1. You have DA creds on a workgroup Windows machine → inject creds → DCSync
2. You're on a low-priv domain account → inject high-priv creds → run PowerView
3. You need to test DA creds without a Linux box available

=== HOW TO USE ===
1. Open CMD/PowerShell with your current privileges
2. Run: runas /netonly /user:INLANEFREIGHT\adunn powershell
3. A password prompt appears — enter adunn's password
4. A new PowerShell window opens
5. In that window, your network auth goes as adunn:
   lsadump::dcsync /domain:INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /user:INLANEFREIGHT\krbtgt

=== GOTCHA: VERIFY IT WORKS ===
Test that creds work before doing sensitive actions:
  dir \\172.16.5.5\SYSVOL
If it lists, the creds are valid and injected correctly.

=== MIMIKATZ VIA RUNAS ===
Inside the runas /netonly PowerShell:
  .\mimikatz.exe
  lsadump::dcsync /domain:INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /user:INLANEFREIGHT\administrator
This runs as your local user BUT authenticates to the DC as adunn.

=== OPSEC ===
Logon type 9 (LOGON_NEW_CREDENTIALS) on the LOCAL machine.
No logon event on the DC until you actually authenticate over the network.
When you do, it appears as a normal Kerberos/NTLM auth from the machine IP.

defense.why_it_works: runas /netonly creates a LOGON32_LOGON_NEW_CREDENTIALS (Logon Type 9) session. The spawned process retains the caller's local token for local operations but presents the injected domain credentials for all network authentication. This bypasses domain-join requirements — any Windows host with network reach to the DC can use domain tools (Mimikatz DCSync, PowerView, net use) as a high-privilege domain account without the machine being domain-joined.
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials in plaintext for the target account. A Windows host (need not be domain-joined) with network connectivity to DC on required ports. runas is a built-in — no additional tools needed. Subsequent network actions (DCSync, PowerView) require their own prerequisites.
defense.impact: Enables all domain tooling to authenticate as a high-privilege account from any Windows machine. Primarily used as a prerequisite step before DCSync, PowerView queries, or other authenticated domain operations when the attacker's machine lacks domain membership or a different user context is required.
defense.detection: Windows Security Event 4648 (A logon was attempted using explicit credentials) on the local host when runas is executed. Subsequent network logons using the injected credentials appear as normal Kerberos/NTLM authentication events (Event 4624 type 3) on DCs and target hosts — indistinguishable from legitimate logons by that user from that machine. EDR may flag the anomalous Logon Type 9 process creation.
defense.artifacts: Event 4648 on the local host with the injected account name; new process tree under the runas context; subsequent authentication events (4624 type 3) on DCs and targets attributed to the injected user from the attacker's machine IP.
defense.prevention: Credential hygiene — avoid exposing DA passwords in plaintext outside password vaults. Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) that enforce no-credential-caching policies. Network segmentation limiting which hosts can reach DC RPC/Kerberos ports. Behavioural detection on Logon Type 9 from non-admin workstations (rare in normal environments).
defense.evasion: runas is a signed Microsoft binary (LOLBin) — unlikely to trigger AV/EDR on process creation alone. Logon Type 9 is uncommon but legitimate (used by some enterprise tools). The DC-side network auth is indistinguishable from a normal workstation logon. Verify creds with a benign read (dir \SYSVOL) before running sensitive tools to avoid failed-logon noise.
defense.misconfiguration: User or computer accounts have been granted AD replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) that should belong exclusively to Domain Controllers. This right allows calling the MS-DRSR (Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol) to retrieve NTLM password hashes for any account — including krbtgt. Typically granted accidentally via WriteDACL on the domain object or through inherited ACEs.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Who has DCSync rights:
Get-ObjectAcl -DistinguishedName 'DC=corp,DC=local' -ResolveGUIDs |
    Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes'} |
    Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights

# Dangerous: any non-DC account appearing here
# CORP\svc_monitoring  DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All  <- not a DC
defense.secure_config:
# Remove non-DC replication rights:
# Using PowerView:
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=corp,DC=local' \
    -PrincipalIdentity 'svc_monitoring' -Rights DCSync

# Monitor with Event 4662 (Object access with properties):
# Filter for: ObjectType = DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All GUID
# {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}
# Any 4662 from non-DC account with this GUID = DCSync in progress

# Microsoft Defender for Identity: built-in 'DCSync attack' alert
# Anomalous AD replication from non-DC IPs also caught by MDI
